kurals.tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் என்னும் கழிபெருங் காரிகை
உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannottam ennum kazhiperung kaarikai
Unmaiyaan undiv vulagu.
kurals.meaning: The world keeps going only because there exists that surpassingly great beauty called kannottam, a kindly, gracious regard for others.
kurals.elementary: Think of a playground where the big kids notice the little ones and help them up when they fall. That kind look makes the whole playground a happy place. Valluvar says the whole world keeps going because people, especially leaders, look at others kindly like that.
kurals.university: The chapter title கண்ணோட்டம் literally means ‘the running (ஓட்டம்) of the eye (கண்)’, i.e., the eye going out towards another in consideration; Parimelazhagar defines it as the disposition that, on seeing those one is familiar with, cannot bring itself to refuse or hurt them, and he places the chapter in the Arasiyal (royal) section as a quality of the king. The phrase கழிபெருங் காரிகை (‘exceedingly great beauty’) treats benignity as an ornament rather than a duty, a theme picked up again in kural 575. The second line, உண்மையான் உண்டு இவ்வுலகு (‘because of its existence, this world exists’), is a strong ontological claim: social order itself depends on this quality. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah) gloss it as ‘looking at a person’s face’ and softening accordingly, while Kalaignar reads it more broadly as love joined with compassion. The text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (கண்ணோட்ட மென்னுங் … யுண்மையா னுண்டிவ்) with no change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Valmiki Ramayana, Rama is repeatedly praised as priyadarśana, ‘pleasing to behold’, and his rule (Rama-rajya) is remembered as an age in which subjects flourished under a king whose regard for them was constant and kindly.
hinduism.explanation: The Indian ideal of the king includes not only just law but a gracious, approachable presence that makes subjects feel seen and protected.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise makes the ruler’s kindly regard the ‘great beauty’ on which the world rests.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 1 (description of Rama’s qualities); tradition of Rama-rajya
hinduism._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel on the gracious king; the Ramayana does not state that the world exists because of this quality.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus grounds human mercy in the character of God, making it the family likeness of all who belong to him.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat kindly regard as the foundational quality, not an optional extra, in ordering human life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the priority of mercy but lacks the Kural’s image of the eye and its claim that the world depends on it.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells the Prophet that his gentleness held the community together, and that harshness would have scattered it.
islam.tie_back: Just as Valluvar says the world stands by kannottam, this verse says a leader’s community stands by his leniency.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: a leader’s gentleness is what keeps society intact.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Priestly Blessing (Birkat Kohanim) pictures divine favour as a shining, lifted face turned towards the people, and makes that gracious look the source of peace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘look of the eye’ that sustains the world is closely mirrored in the blessing’s gracious face that grants peace.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the gracious face as source of well-being; it is God’s face rather than a king’s.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, the Buddha, moved by compassion for beings, surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha and saw beings with little dust in their eyes, and so decided to teach.
buddhism.explanation: In the Pali account the Buddha’s decision to teach springs from a compassionate look over the whole world.
buddhism.tie_back: Like kannottam, it is a compassionate gaze that sets in motion the good of the world.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Nice fit on the compassionate gaze; the context is teaching the Dhamma rather than governance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “from whose eyes as they glanced flowed love that unnerves the limbs: and beautiful is their glance beneath their brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the three Graces (Charites), daughters of Zeus, whose gracious glance is itself their beauty and pours out love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘great beauty’ located in a kindly look is the same idea as the Graces whose beauty lies in their glance.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Striking match on the beauty of the glance; the Graces’ love is more charm than moral benignity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca, addressing the young Nero, argues that clemency befits no one more than a king, because a ruler’s mercy is what binds subjects to him and keeps the state secure.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, mercy is the defining ornament of rightful power and the practical foundation of a stable realm.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Seneca treats the ruler’s gentleness as both his chief beauty and what holds the world together.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in political context; Seneca speaks of clemency toward offenders, a narrower sense than kannottam.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல் அஃதிலார்
உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannottath thulladhu ulagiyal aqdhilaar
Unmai nilakkup porai.
kurals.meaning: All the ordinary business of the world runs on kindly regard; people who lack it merely exist as a burden on the earth.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a class where everyone shares pencils and helps each other. One child never helps anyone and only takes. The class works because of the helpers; the one who never helps just makes things heavier for everyone. Valluvar says people without kindness are like extra weight the earth has to carry.
kurals.university: உலகியல் means ‘the conduct or course of the world’, i.e., everyday social transactions, and Parimelazhagar takes the first line to mean that all such dealings are sustained by kannottam. The second line’s உண்மை (‘existence’, not ‘truth’ here) and பொறை (‘burden’) make a stark judgement: a person without kindly regard contributes nothing and simply weighs on the land, an image the Tamil tradition also uses of the ungrateful and the idle. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both render பொறை as சுமை/பாரம் (load), while Kalaignar stresses the ‘embracing with love’ that such people lack. The couplet thus moves from the cosmic claim of 571 to its negative corollary. ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org agree; the latter prints the sandhi-joined form (துள்ள துலகிய லஃதிலா / ருண்மை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…nonviolence; truthfulness; freedom from anger; renunciation; tranquillity; aversion to faultfinding; compassion for all living entities; freedom from covetousness; gentleness…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists dayā bhūteṣu (compassion toward all beings) and mārdava (gentleness) among the qualities of the divine nature (daivī sampat).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, sees compassion as the mark of a life that upholds the world rather than burdens it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Clear overlap on compassion; the Gita does not use the image of a burden on the earth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, a fig tree that bears no fruit is said only to take up space and exhaust the soil.
christianity.tie_back: The fruitless tree that ‘cumbers the ground’ is almost exactly the Kural’s person without kindness who is a burden on the earth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close image of useless existence burdening the ground; the parable concerns repentance generally, not kindness specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will not be merciful to those who are not merciful to mankind.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes mercy toward people the condition for receiving God’s mercy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts judge the person lacking kindly regard as having no rightful place, whether on earth or before God.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the severity toward the unmerciful; the hadith looks to divine judgement rather than social usefulness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much; and receive all men with a pleasant countenance.”
judaism.explanation: Even the famously strict Shammai required that every person be received with a pleasant face, making warm regard a basic rule of social life.
judaism.tie_back: Receiving everyone with a kindly face is the everyday ‘worldly conduct’ that the Kural says rests on kannottam.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on kindly countenance as a social norm; lacks the ‘burden on the earth’ judgement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life / Her child, her only child, / So with a boundless heart / Should one cherish all living beings”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta asks for a boundless, protective kindness toward every being without exception.
buddhism.tie_back: This all-embracing goodwill is what the Kural says the whole world runs on.
buddhism.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (trans. Amaravati Sangha)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the universal scope of kindness; not framed as the basis of social order.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus and Hermes, disguised as travellers, are turned away by every house in a Phrygian village except that of the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon; the gods flood the pitiless village and turn the couple’s hut into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s tale shows the unkind community swept away while the kindly household is preserved and honoured.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The villagers without regard for strangers are, as the Kural says, a burden the earth can do without.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit; the virtue at issue is hospitality, a close cousin of kannottam.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… as men, too, are born for the sake of men, that they may be able mutually to help one another; in this direction we ought to follow Nature as our guide, to contribute to the general good by an interchange of acts of kindness, by giving and receiving …”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says human society is held together by mutual kindness, and a few sections later calls those who keep to their own affairs and give society nothing traitors to social life.
philosophy.tie_back: As in the Kural, the world's business runs on kindly regard, and those who withhold it contribute nothing to the life they share.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §§22, 29 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, De Officiis I.20-41); the quoted words are from §22, and §29 is paraphrased in the explanation. Strong match on kindness as the bond of society; Cicero's 'traitors to social life' is close to, but less stark than, the Kural's 'burden on the earth'.

kurals.tamil:
பண்என்னாம் பாடற்கு இயைபின்றேல் கண்என்னாம்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pan ennaam paadarku iyaipindrel kan ennaam
Kannottam illaadha kan.
kurals.meaning: What use is a melody that does not fit the song? Just so, what use is an eye that has no kindly regard in it?
kurals.elementary: If someone plays a happy tune while you sing a sad lullaby, the music doesn’t help at all; it just sounds wrong. Valluvar says eyes are the same: eyes are meant to look kindly, and eyes without kindness are like music that doesn’t match the song.
kurals.university: பண் is the technical term for a melodic mode in Tamil music (roughly comparable to a raga), and இயைபு means ‘concordance’ or ‘fitting together’; the couplet thus draws on the Tamil musical tradition, in which the right pann had to suit the song and its mood. Parimelazhagar explains that just as a pann not matched to its song is useless, an eye not joined to kannottam is useless, so kindness is the eye’s proper ‘accompaniment’. The rhetorical question என்னாம் (‘what will it be?’, i.e., of what use) is repeated to link the two halves. Solomon Pappaiah renders பண் as ராகம், and all four commentaries on ytamizh.com share this reading. thirukkural-thamizh.org has பண்ணென்னாம் … கியைபின்றேற் for ytamizh’s பண்என்னாம் … இயைபின்றேல், which are orthographic and sandhi differences only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bharata’s Natyashastra teaches that music and performance succeed only when they evoke the right rasa (aesthetic emotion) through fitting bhava (feeling); technically correct sound without the fitting emotion fails to move the audience.
hinduism.explanation: Indian aesthetics judges art by whether its form fits and conveys the right inner feeling.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s mismatched pann and song is exactly this failure of fit, and the eye without kindness is form without its proper feeling.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallels only the musical half of the simile; no moral teaching about eyes or kindness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says even the most eloquent gift, if it lacks love, is only empty noise.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s musical image of noise without love matches the Kural’s melody without fit and eye without kindness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Remarkably close structure (musical image plus missing love); the organ in question is the tongue, not the eye.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury as does one who spends his wealth [only] to be seen by the people…”
islam.explanation: The Quran warns that a gift given with hurtful words or reminders is emptied of value, like dust washed off a bare rock.
islam.tie_back: An outward act without inner kindness is worthless, just as the Kural says of the eye without kannottam.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of form emptied by lack of kindness; no musical or eye imagery.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.”
judaism.explanation: Amos declares that temple music is unwelcome to God when it is not matched by justice and righteousness in life.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a melody that does not fit its true purpose is worthless; what gives it value is the moral quality behind it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit on music emptied by moral mismatch; the missing quality is justice rather than kindly regard.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares fine words without practice to a flower that looks lovely but has no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: The scentless flower, like the ill-fitting melody and the unkind eye, has the outward form but lacks its essential quality.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same logic of form without essence; concerns speech and practice, not kindness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus’s song in the underworld is so perfectly fitted to his grief that it moves even the pitiless rulers of Hades to pity and to release Eurydice.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the myth music has power because it carries true feeling that softens the hardest hearts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Music matched to feeling moves others to pity; the Kural says eyes, like music, exist to carry that pity.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Links music and pity loosely; it is a positive example, not the Kural’s negative comparison.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that rhythm and harmony sink deep into the soul and that good music must fit and express good character; music detached from virtue is rejected.
philosophy.explanation: Plato ties the worth of music to its harmony with the moral character it expresses.
philosophy.tie_back: As Plato judges music by its fit with character, Valluvar judges the eye by its fit with kindness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘fitting’ principle for music; says nothing about eyes or benignity.

kurals.tamil:
உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் அளவினால்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulapol mugaththevan seyyum alavinaal
Kannottam illaadha kan.
kurals.meaning: Eyes that lack kindly regard in due measure only seem to be present in the face; beyond that, what good do they do?
kurals.elementary: A doll can have beautiful painted eyes, but they never notice when you are sad. They are just there for decoration. Valluvar says eyes that never look kindly at anyone are like doll’s eyes: they are in the face, but they are not really doing an eye’s job.
kurals.university: உளபோல் (‘as if they exist’) makes the eyes a mere appearance on the face (முகத்து), and எவன் செய்யும் asks what use they serve. The key qualifier is அளவினால் (‘in due measure’): Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the kindness required as kannottam within proper limits, i.e., kindness that does not override duty, which anticipates kural 578. Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ‘kannottam within bounds’ (வரம்பிற்கு உட்பட்ட), while Kalaignar reads it as the eyes failing to stir love and pity in the heart. The couplet shares its second line verbatim with 573 (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), a deliberate repetition that ties the two images together. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints உளபோன் … மளவினாற் (sandhi forms) for ytamizh’s உளபோல் … அளவினால், with no change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But you cannot see Me with your present eyes. Therefore I give you divine eyes. Behold My mystic opulence!”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that his physical eyes, though working, cannot see what truly matters until he is given a higher kind of sight.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that physical eyes alone are not enough; the eye has worth only when it sees in the right way.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘eyes that do not truly see’ idea; the higher sight is spiritual vision, not kindness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the eye’s moral quality (a ‘single’ or generous eye versus an ‘evil’ or grudging eye) determines whether a person is full of light or darkness.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Jesus judges the eye by the disposition it carries, not by its mere presence.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close: in Jewish idiom the ‘evil eye’ is ungenerous; the Kural’s ‘due measure’ nuance is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that outward features count for nothing before God; what matters is the heart and what it produces.
islam.tie_back: Eyes that merely sit in the face without kindness are exactly the outward form this hadith says has no value.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the face-versus-heart contrast; does not speak specifically about the eye or kindly regard.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said, a good eye; Rabbi Joshua said, a good companion; Rabbi Yose said, a good neighbor; Rabbi Shimon said, foresight. Rabbi Elazar said, a good heart.”
judaism.explanation: Asked for the right way to cleave to, Rabban Yohanan’s disciples name the ‘good eye’ (ayin tovah), a generous and benevolent way of looking at others, and its opposite, the evil eye, as the way to shun.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis, like Valluvar, make the moral quality of one’s gaze a central measure of character.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the ‘good eye’ as benevolence; the Kural’s ‘due measure’ qualification is not discussed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha reminds the over-strenuous monk Sona, a former lute player, that a lute sounds well only when its strings are neither too tight nor too loose, and tells him to set his effort in the same balance.
buddhism.explanation: Right practice, like right tuning, depends on measure rather than excess in either direction.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s அளவினால் (‘in due measure’) asks for kindness tuned in exactly this balanced way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallels only the ‘measure’ element; the topic is effort in meditation, not kindness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Argus Panoptes, the giant with a hundred eyes, is set by Hera to watch Io and never lets all his eyes sleep, yet uses them only for guarding and surveillance, never for pity.
greek_mythology.explanation: The many-eyed watchman sees everything but feels nothing for the captive he guards, and is finally lulled to sleep and slain by Hermes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Argus shows that eyes, however many, are useless as eyes of a person when they carry no kindness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An illustrative contrast rather than a teaching; the myth does not moralise about kindness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Emmanuel Levinas holds that the face of another person makes an ethical demand on me before anything else; to see a face truly is already to be called to responsibility for the other.
philosophy.explanation: For Levinas, ethics begins in the face-to-face encounter, where looking at someone properly means responding to their vulnerability.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s eyes that merely sit in the face without responding to others fail exactly the encounter Levinas places at the root of ethics.
philosophy.source: Emmanuel Levinas, Totality and Infinity (1961), Section III
philosophy._accuracy_note: Deep conceptual parallel on seeing and responsibility; Levinas’s phenomenology is far removed from the Kural’s royal context.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணிற்கு அணிகலம் கண்ணோட்டம் அஃதின்றேல்
புண்ணென்று உணரப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannirku anigalam kannottam aqdhindrel
Punnendru unarap padum.
kurals.meaning: Kindly regard is the jewel that adorns the eye; without it the eyes will be seen as nothing more than two sores.
kurals.elementary: People wear necklaces and bracelets to look nice. Valluvar says the nicest thing your eyes can ‘wear’ is kindness. If your eyes are always angry or cold, people will not see pretty eyes at all; they will see something that hurts, like a scrape.
kurals.university: அணிகலம் (‘ornament, jewel’) recalls the காரிகை (‘beauty’) of 571: kannottam is the eye’s jewellery, not merely its function. The shocking alternative, புண் (‘wound, sore’), plays on the near-rhyme கண்/புண், and the passive உணரப்படும் (‘will be perceived as’) implies the judgement of others; Solomon Pappaiah specifies ‘by the wise’ (பெரியோரால்), as does the Pope/Drew-style English gloss on ytamizh. Parimelazhagar’s point is that eyes are honoured only because they carry grace; without it they are merely openings in the flesh. This is the couplet the chapter is most remembered for, and its imagery of ornament versus wound is found in later Tamil ethical literature. The two sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கண்ணிற் கணிகலங் … மஃதின்றேற் / புண்ணென் றுணரப்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Adi Shankara’s Kanakadhara Stotram, the poet praises the gracious sidelong glance (kaṭākṣa) of the goddess Lakshmi, whose kindly look alone is said to shower prosperity on a poor household.
hinduism.explanation: In Hindu devotion the deity’s kindly glance is itself the gift and the adornment of divine beauty.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hymn treats the kindly look as the eye’s true jewel and source of blessing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on the gracious glance as beauty and blessing; lacks the Kural’s warning image of the sore.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest…”
christianity.explanation: Before challenging the rich young man, Jesus looks at him with love, so that even a hard word comes through a kindly gaze.
christianity.tie_back: This is kannottam in action: the eye’s true adornment is the love it carries toward the person it looks at.
christianity._accuracy_note: Concrete example of a loving look; not a general teaching about the eye’s ornament.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your smiling in the face of your brother is charity…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts even a smile toward another as an act of charity (sadaqah).
islam.tie_back: A kindly face is itself a gift, just as the Kural calls kindly regard the eye’s jewel.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the moral value of a kindly face; no ornament-versus-sore contrast.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew is tov ayin, literally ‘good of eye’, the biblical idiom for a generous, kindly disposition toward others.
judaism.tie_back: The ‘good eye’ that is blessed is a close Hebrew counterpart to the kindly eye that the Kural calls adorned.
judaism._accuracy_note: Idiom matches remarkably (a good eye); focus is generosity rather than gracious regard as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings. The devas protect one. Neither fire, poison, nor weapons can touch one. One’s mind gains concentration quickly. One’s complexion is bright.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the eleven benefits of cultivating goodwill (metta), the Buddha lists being dear to others and having a bright, clear complexion.
buddhism.tie_back: Goodwill brightens the face and makes one beloved, just as kannottam is the ornament of the eye.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 11.16, Metta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that kindness beautifies the face; no reference to eyes specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Cyclops Polyphemus, with his single great eye, looks on Odysseus and his men not as guests but as food; Odysseus blinds that eye with a burning stake and escapes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s monster embodies the eye without regard for guests, and his punishment falls on the very eye that showed no kindness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyphemus’s pitiless eye, turned into a wound, is a vivid picture of the Kural’s eye without kannottam becoming a sore.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Imagistically striking but a narrative contrast, not a moral statement about kindness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes a nameless virtue of social life, a kind of friendliness, the mean between the obsequious flatterer and the quarrelsome, surly person who cares nothing for giving pain to others.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the pleasant, considerate manner in dealings with others is a genuine virtue, and its absence makes one disagreeable.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s friendly mean is close to kannottam as the grace of social interaction, whose lack makes a person offensive to others.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good fit on considerate manner as a virtue; Aristotle does not use eye imagery.

kurals.tamil:
மண்ணோ டியைந்த மரத்தனையர் கண்ணோ
டியைந்துகண் ணோடா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mannodu iyaindha maraththanaiyar kannodu
iyaindhukan nodaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who have eyes yet never look kindly on others are like trees rooted in the soil: they have the form but not the feeling.
kurals.elementary: A tree stands in one place and can’t notice when someone near it is crying. Valluvar says a person who has eyes but never looks kindly at others is just like that tree: standing there, but not really caring about anyone.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a careful parallel: மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரம் (‘a tree joined to the soil’) and கண்ணோடு இயைந்து கண்ணோடாதவர் (‘those who, though joined to eyes, do not let the eye run out [in kindness]’). The verb கண்ணோடு is the root of the chapter’s title, so the line plays on having கண் (eyes) but not doing கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar is usually cited as noting that trees too were said to have ‘eyes’ (buds or nodes), so that the unkind are no better than eyed trees; this pun is reported in commentary tradition and should be treated with some caution. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘like a tree that has eyes but does not see’, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses that such people move about but are as insensible as a tree fixed in the earth. The two texts agree word for word, with the line break falling inside கண்ணோ / டியைந்து in both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita lists pāruṣya (harshness, hardness) among the traits of the āsurī (demonic) nature, the opposite of the gentle divine nature.
hinduism.tie_back: The hard, unfeeling person the Kural likens to a tree is the Gita’s harsh āsuric type.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the condemnation of harshness; the tree simile and eye imagery are absent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes his disciples for having working eyes and ears yet failing to perceive what is before them.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Having eyes yet not seeing’ is the same paradox the Kural sets out: joined to eyes, yet not using them as eyes should be used.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same paradox of eyes without true sight; the failure is spiritual understanding, not kindness.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says true blindness lies not in the eyes but in hearts that will not respond.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s tree-like people have seeing eyes but unfeeling hearts, exactly the blindness this verse describes.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on eyes versus heart; the heart’s failure here is to heed signs rather than to show kindness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not… They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm mocks idols of wood and metal that have eyes without sight, and says their makers become like them.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s people with eyes who are no better than trees resemble the Psalm’s lifeless images with unseeing eyes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close image of eyed but insensible objects; the Psalm’s target is idolatry, not unkindness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but, his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares a person who never develops inwardly to an ox that merely grows bigger.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s tree-like person, this one has bodily existence without the inner quality that makes a human being.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘mere physical existence’ comparison; the missing quality is wisdom, not kindness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Gorgon Medusa’s gaze turns everyone who meets it to stone, until Perseus beheads her using a mirrored shield.
greek_mythology.explanation: Medusa’s look is the opposite of a kindly regard: it does not warm or soften others but deadens them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A gaze with no warmth is lifeless and makes others lifeless, like the Kural’s eyed yet wooden people.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose symbolic contrast only; the myth has no moral about benignity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius writes that a branch cut off from the branch next to it is cut off from the whole tree, and so a person who separates himself from even one fellow human has cut himself off from the whole community.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic emperor, withdrawing one’s goodwill from others amounts to self-amputation from the living body of humanity.
philosophy.tie_back: Both use tree imagery to say that a person without fellow-feeling is cut off from true human life.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Tree imagery and social point align, though Marcus’s branch is severed rather than rooted.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர் கண்ணுடையார்
கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannottam illavar kannilar kannudaiyaar
Kannottam inmaiyum il.
kurals.meaning: People without kindly regard are really eyeless; and those who truly have eyes are never without kindly regard.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your friend drops their lunch and everyone looks away, but one kid runs over to help. Valluvar would say only that kid truly ‘saw’. Having real eyes means noticing people and caring about them; if you never care, it is as if you have no eyes at all.
kurals.university: The couplet is a chiasmus built on the single word கண்: those without கண்ணோட்டம் are கண்ணிலர் (‘eyeless’), and those who are கண்ணுடையார் (‘possessed of eyes’) are never without கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar reads it as a definition by convertibility: in the moral sense, having eyes and having kannottam are one and the same thing, so that physical sight without kindness does not count as sight. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it almost identically, while Kalaignar reverses the emphasis, saying the eyes of the compassionate alone deserve the name. With 576 it completes a sequence (573-577) that systematically strips the unkind eye of every value. Both sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has sandhi forms கண்ணோட்ட மில்லவர் … மின்மையு மில்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita says the truly wise are sama-darśinaḥ, ‘those who see with equal vision’, regarding every being with the same respect.
hinduism.tie_back: For both texts, real seeing is a moral kind of sight; only the one who regards all beings rightly truly has eyes.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on true seeing as right regard for others; equal vision stresses impartiality more than warmth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.”
christianity.explanation: In the Gospels, Jesus’ seeing the crowds leads directly into compassion.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in narrative form: one who truly sees cannot be without compassion.
christianity._accuracy_note: A clear case of seeing that turns into compassion; not stated as a general principle.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes those who have working senses but do not use them rightly as worse than cattle.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says people with eyes that do not truly see are in effect eyeless.
islam._accuracy_note: Same paradox of seeing eyes that do not see; the failure is spiritual heedlessness rather than unkindness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good eye, a humble spirit and a moderate appetite he is of the disciples of Abraham, our father. An evil eye, a haughty spirit and a limitless appetite he is of the disciples of Balaam, the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah makes the ‘good eye’, a generous and kindly way of seeing others, the first mark of a true disciple of Abraham.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the eye that counts is the good, benevolent eye; the other kind belongs to the wicked.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the benevolent eye as defining identity; lacks the chiasmus of eyeless versus eyed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha speaks of three eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of discernment, and teaches that the eye of discernment is the highest.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching separates physical sight from the higher ‘eyes’ that see truly.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise separates the physical eye from the true eye, which in his case is the eye of kindness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the distinction of physical and true eyes; the highest eye is wisdom, not kindness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, the blind prophet Tiresias sees the truth, while Oedipus, with perfect eyesight, cannot see what he has done until he blinds himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play turns on the irony that the sighted man is truly blind and the blind man truly sees.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s paradox that the sighted can be ‘eyeless’ has its Greek counterpart in Oedipus and Tiresias.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel paradox of sight and blindness; the true sight is knowledge of fate, not kindness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He is a runaway, who flies from social reason; he is blind, who shuts the eyes of the understanding; … he is a piece rent asunder from the state, who tears his own soul from that of reasonable animals, which is one.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus lists the ways a person fails his own nature: whoever cuts himself off from the shared reason and fellowship of rational beings is a fugitive, blind, and torn from the whole.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Marcus calls the one who withdraws from fellow-feeling blind, though his blindness is of the understanding rather than a lack of kindly regard.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV, §29 (tr. George Long)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long); the ellipsis omits one clause. Next-best match: the shared image is blindness in one who cuts himself off from others, but Marcus's emphasis is on social reason, not on graciousness or compassion.

kurals.tamil:
கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்க்கு
உரிமை உடைத்திவ் வுலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Karumam sidhaiyaamal kannoda vallaarkku
Urimai udaiththiv vulagu.
kurals.meaning: The world rightfully belongs to those who can show kindly regard without letting their duty be damaged.
kurals.elementary: A good referee is friendly and kind to all the players, but still calls a foul when someone breaks the rules. Valluvar says the best leaders are like that: kind to everyone, but they never let kindness stop them from doing what is right.
kurals.university: கருமம் here means one’s proper task, and for a king Parimelazhagar specifies it as the administration of justice (the ytamizh English gloss adds ‘administration of justice’ in brackets); சிதையாமல் means ‘without letting it be spoiled’. The couplet thus sets a limit on kannottam: kindness toward familiar people must never become favouritism that ruins just government, which explains the அளவினால் (‘in due measure’) of 574. உரிமை உடைத்து இவ்வுலகு (‘this world has rightful ownership [for them]’) promises that such rulers are the world’s natural possessors. Modern commentators generalise the principle to anyone who is compassionate without neglecting their duties (Kalaignar: ‘first in not failing duty and in showering mercy’). Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கருமஞ் சிதையாமற் … வல்லார்க் / குரிமை யுடைத்திவ்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that a king severe with the rod terrifies his subjects, one too mild with it is despised, and one who wields it justly is respected.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra demands a balance: neither harshness nor softness, but punishment measured by justice.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s balance of kindness that does not ruin duty, seen from the side of the king’s rod.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same balance between mildness and justice; Kautilya frames it around punishment rather than kindness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee? She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus shows mercy to the woman accused of adultery while still clearly naming the wrong and calling her to change.
christianity.tie_back: Mercy without abandoning the moral standard is exactly the Kural’s kindness that does not damage duty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit of mercy joined with moral firmness; the passage is not about rulers.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression.”
islam.explanation: The Quran joins ʿadl (justice) and iḥsān (excellence or kindness) in a single command, so that neither is to be sacrificed to the other.
islam.tie_back: Justice held together with kindness is the combination the Kural says wins the world.
islam._accuracy_note: Pairs justice and kindness closely; does not explicitly say kindness must not undermine justice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that a king’s rule is secured by mercy (ḥesed) together with truth.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural says the world belongs to the ruler who is kind without neglecting duty, Proverbs says mercy with truth upholds the throne.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close royal parallel of mercy plus truth securing rule.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Jatakas list ten royal virtues (dasa raja dhamma) for a righteous king, including generosity, gentleness (maddava), patience (khanti) and non-violence, alongside moral conduct and adherence to what is right.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist ideal king combines gentleness and patience with steady righteousness.
buddhism.tie_back: This list of royal virtues pairs kindness with righteousness, just as the Kural does.
buddhism.source: Jataka 534 (Mahahamsa Jataka) and related Jataka tradition of dasa raja dhamma
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit for rulers; the list is not framed as a limit on kindness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena founds the Areopagus court to try Orestes and then persuades the vengeful Furies to accept honour in Athens, turning them into the ‘Kindly Ones’ without abolishing justice.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows justice kept intact while vengeance is softened into benevolence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Athena achieves what the Kural praises: kindness that does not destroy the work of justice.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel in balancing justice and kindness; the setting is civic, not personal regard.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes equity (epieikeia) as a correction of the law where its generality makes it unjust, and the equitable person as one who takes less than his strict due though the law is on his side.
philosophy.explanation: Equity lets humane judgement soften the law without abandoning justice itself.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s equity is the kind of measured mildness the Kural asks for: kind, yet never spoiling justice.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close conceptual match; equity concerns legal judgement more than personal kindness.

kurals.tamil:
ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்கண் ணோடிப்
பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Oruththaatrum panbinaar kannum kannodip
Poruththaatrum panbe thalai.
kurals.meaning: The highest virtue is to show kindly regard and patiently bear with even those whose nature is to hurt us.
kurals.elementary: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, the easy thing is to be mean back. Valluvar says the very best thing is to stay kind and patient with them anyway. That is the hardest kind of kindness, and so it is the greatest.
kurals.university: ஒறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பினார் means ‘those whose nature is to cause harm/afflict’, and the matching பொறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பு is ‘the nature that bears it and carries on’; the verbal rhyme ஒறுத்து/பொறுத்து sets the injurer’s nature against the forbearer’s. கண்ணும் (‘even towards’) extends kannottam from familiar friends to enemies, the chapter’s highest reach. Commentators differ slightly on the object: Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘even those who deserve punishment’, stressing a judge’s leniency, while Solomon Pappaiah and the English gloss read ‘those who grieve or harm us’, stressing personal forbearance; Parimelazhagar’s royal reading allows both. தலை (‘head’, i.e., foremost) ranks this above all other forms of kindness. Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has கண்ணுங்கண் for ytamizh’s கண்ணும்கண்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the devotee dear to him as maitraḥ karuṇaḥ (friendly and compassionate) and kṣamī (forgiving) toward all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Kindness and forbearance toward all, including those who harm us, is the Kural’s supreme virtue.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on universal friendliness and forgiveness; enemies are not named explicitly in the verse itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
christianity.explanation: On the cross, Jesus prays for the very people who are putting him to death.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s highest virtue at its limit: kindly bearing with those who are actively harming one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-perfect illustration of forbearing kindness toward those who afflict one.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Quran commands answering hostility with something better, promising that an enemy may become a close friend.
islam.tie_back: Returning kindness for harm is exactly the forbearing kannottam the Kural ranks highest.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on responding to enmity with goodness.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who was plagued by a heretic and waited for the moment of divine anger to curse him, but dozed off; on waking he concluded that cursing people is not proper, since God’s mercy is over all his creatures, even sinners.
judaism.explanation: The sage learns that even toward someone who torments him, the right course is mercy rather than retaliation.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbi Yehoshua’s turn from cursing to forbearance is the Kural’s kindly patience toward those who harm us.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit; the sage’s restraint comes by providence rather than by his own initial choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches meeting each vice with its opposite virtue rather than in kind.
buddhism.tie_back: Overcoming the wicked by goodness is the Kural’s forbearing kindness toward those who hurt us.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on answering harm with goodness; framed as ‘overcoming’ rather than patient bearing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the aged Priam comes by night to Achilles’ tent to ransom the body of Hector, the son who killed Patroclus, Achilles, moved by pity, weeps with him, returns the body and grants a truce for the funeral.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest warrior of the Iliad extends compassion to the father of his worst enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ pity for Priam is kindly regard shown to one bound up with the very person who hurt him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Powerful example of compassion toward an enemy; not presented as a general virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that benevolence is invincible if it is genuine, and that the most insolent man can do nothing to one who stays kind to him and gently corrects him.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, unshakeable goodwill toward offenders is both the highest and the strongest stance.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus’s invincible kindness toward those who wrong us is the Kural’s supreme forbearance.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit; Marcus stresses gentle correction as well as bearing.

kurals.tamil:
பெயக்கண்டும் நஞ்சுண் டமைவர் நயத்தக்க
நாகரிகம் வேண்டு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Peyakkandum nanjundu amaivar nayaththakka
Naagarigam vendu pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who seek the courtesy that everyone admires will even drink poison they have seen poured for them by a friend, and stay at peace with that friend.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a friend gives you a cookie that tastes awful, and you know they didn’t make it right. A very gracious person might eat it and still smile, because they care more about the friend than the cookie. Valluvar tells this as an extreme story to show how far true kindness can go.
kurals.university: The couplet is deliberately hyperbolic: பெயக் கண்டும் (‘even having seen it poured’) and நஞ்சு உண்டு அமைவர் (‘they drink the poison and remain calm/content’) describe people who knowingly accept harm from someone close rather than break the bond. நாகரிகம் here does not mean modern ‘civilisation’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take it as the refined kannottam, the urbane courtesy that is நயத்தக்க (‘worthy of being desired’ by all). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah specify that the poison is offered by those one has long associated with, and the Sangam anthology Natrinai (poem 355) is frequently cited for the closely related idea that the truly refined will drink even poison offered by friends. Commentators treat the couplet as illustrating the extreme limit of kannottam rather than a literal instruction. Both texts agree word for word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gods and demons churn the ocean of milk, the deadly poison halahala rises first and threatens all the worlds; out of compassion Shiva drinks it and holds it in his throat, which turns blue, earning him the name Nilakantha.
hinduism.explanation: Shiva knowingly takes poison upon himself for the sake of others, showing the highest kind of grace.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the refined person of the Kural, Shiva drinks poison he has seen, calmly, out of care for others.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong image of knowingly drinking poison out of compassion; it is not offered by a friend.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.”
christianity.explanation: At the Last Supper Jesus, knowing Judas will betray him, still shares food with him as a sign of fellowship.
christianity.tie_back: Keeping table fellowship with one known to be preparing harm is the Kural’s courtesy that drinks the poison a companion pours.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in the knowing acceptance of a false friend; no literal poison, and the roles of giver and receiver are reversed.

islam.quote_or_event: “A Jewess brought a poisoned (cooked) sheep for the Prophet (ﷺ) who ate from it. She was brought to the Prophet and he was asked, ‘Shall we kill her?’ He said, ‘No.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet was served poisoned meat, suffered its effects, and still refused to have the woman who served it killed.
islam.tie_back: Enduring poison served by a host and refusing revenge is a striking historical parallel to the Kural’s image.
islam._accuracy_note: Remarkable literal parallel; the Prophet did not knowingly eat the poison, and the giver was not a friend.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph, once sold into slavery by his own brothers, forgives them and promises to provide for them.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph swallowed the ‘poison’ his kin gave him and still kept the bond, which is the Kural’s gracious courtesy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on kindness toward kin who did harm; the poison image is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: At Pava the smith Cunda serves the Buddha a dish (sukara-maddava) after which he falls gravely ill; the Buddha eats it, then asks Ananda to reassure Cunda that the last meal given to a Buddha brings great merit, so that no one blames him.
buddhism.explanation: Even as the meal leads to his final illness, the Buddha’s concern is to protect his host from remorse and blame.
buddhism.tie_back: Accepting a harmful dish from a devoted host while guarding the bond is close to the Kural’s image of drinking a friend’s poison calmly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close narrative parallel; the food was not maliciously poisoned.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The wise centaur Chiron, teacher and friend of heroes, is accidentally struck by one of Heracles’ arrows dipped in the Hydra’s poison; unable to heal, he bears it without enmity toward Heracles and finally gives up his immortality.
greek_mythology.explanation: Chiron endures a poison that came from a friend’s hand without turning against him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Chiron bearing poison from a friend without resentment echoes the Kural’s refined person who drinks poison from a companion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match: the poisoning was accidental, and the sources do not stress courtesy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedo, the servant of the Eleven who brings Socrates the hemlock weeps as he says farewell, and Socrates speaks warmly of the man’s kindness before calmly drinking the cup.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates meets the bearer of his poison with graciousness and drinks it with complete composure.
philosophy.tie_back: His calm, courteous acceptance of the cup is a classical image of the Kural’s refinement that drinks poison and stays at peace.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong image of composure and courtesy before poison; the jailer is not a friend who wishes him harm.
